nameStory: The hexagonal-pored polypore gets its name from the distinctive six-sided shapes of its tiny pores underneath the cap. While most bracket fungi have round pores, this species creates a honeycomb-like pattern that looks almost geometric, as if nature was practicing its geometry skills!
description: This bracket fungus forms yellowish to orange, scaly shelves that jut out from dead hardwood logs and branches. The caps have a distinctly rough, almost shaggy texture from overlapping scales. What makes this polypore special is flipping it over to reveal the honeycomb pattern of hexagonal or diamond-shaped pores underneath. It's a medium-sized bracket that helps break down dead wood as part of nature's recycling crew.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: The undersurface shows distinctive hexagonal or diamond-shaped pores that look like tiny geometric cells, quite different from the round pores of most bracket fungi

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Yellowish to bright orange cap covered in overlapping scales that feel rough and bumpy to the touch, giving it a shaggy appearance

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always found on dead hardwood logs, branches, or sticks - never on living trees or conifers

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Forms shelf-like brackets that project horizontally from wood, often in overlapping clusters

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens may have a mild, pleasant mushroomy smell without any strong or unpleasant odors

habitat: Look for this fungus on fallen hardwood logs and dead branches in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England. It particularly favors oak, maple, and other broad-leaved trees in moist woodland areas. You'll often find it along hiking trails where dead wood is abundant, from lowland forests up to mid-elevation slopes.

seasonality.spring: Fresh growth begins as temperatures warm, with new brackets appearing bright orange and actively growing on dead wood.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most vibrant colors and fresh specimens, especially after periods of rain and humidity.
seasonality.fall: Mature brackets become more weathered but remain identifiable, often developing darker colors as they age.
seasonality.winter: Old brackets persist on logs and may become faded and brittle, but the distinctive hexagonal pore pattern remains visible.

funFact: This fungus was once thought to be found across three continents, but scientists recently discovered that North American specimens are actually a completely different species - proving that even fungi can have cases of mistaken identity that fool experts for decades!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other orange bracket fungi, but the hexagonal pores are a dead giveaway - just remember 'hex for hexagonal' and flip it over to check. Other polypores will have round pores that look like tiny circles, not geometric shapes.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name recently changed as DNA studies revealed that what scientists thought was one widespread species was actually several distinct species. North American specimens previously called this species are now classified as Neofavolus americanus, showing how modern molecular techniques are rewriting fungal family trees.
compareHints: Neofavolus americanus, the closely related North American species, looks nearly identical but genetic studies show they're distinct species. Neofavolus suavissimus tends to have a sweeter smell and slightly different coloration. The hexagonal pores remain the best field characteristic to distinguish this genus from other bracket fungi, regardless of which exact Neofavolus species you've found.
